# Week 5, Day 2.1 - Prerequisites check

Today you write a function Playwright runs **once**, before any test. One new TypeScript idea,
two Node ideas you have met.

| Concept | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `async` / `await`, Promises | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `import path from "node:path"` | [week4/day4_1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) |
| Type-only imports | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `export default` a **function** | extends [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) - below |

**Next:** [Day 2.2 - Logging in once](/learn/w5/d2/p2)

## Concept 1 - `export default` a function

You met `export default` in [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1), exporting a config *object*.
Same keyword, and a module can nominate only one such value - but here the value is a **function**,
which is what makes it callable. `globalSetup` requires exactly this: point the config at a file,
and Playwright calls whatever that file's default export is.

```ts
export default async function globalSetup() { ... }     // named, and default
export default async () => { ... };                     // anonymous
```

Prefer the first. The name shows up in stack traces - which matters when setup is what broke.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 2 - a path that works on any machine

Never write `"week5/generated/.auth/state.json"` in a config. `path.join` uses the right
separator for the OS, and `__dirname` anchors it to *this file* rather than to wherever the
command was run from.

| Expression | Gives |
|---|---|
| `__dirname` | the folder holding the current file |
| `path.join(__dirname, ".auth", "s.json")` | `...\generated\.auth\s.json` on Windows |
| `"./.auth/s.json"` | relative to the **shell's** cwd - breaks when CI runs from elsewhere |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 3 - the `FullConfig` type

Your setup function receives the resolved config. You rarely need it, but typing the parameter
documents that it exists:

```ts
import { type FullConfig } from "@playwright/test";

export default async function globalSetup(_config: FullConfig): Promise<void> { ... }
```

The leading underscore in `_config` is the convention for *deliberately unused*, and it stops
some lint rules from complaining.

**Next:** [Day 2.2 - Logging in once](/learn/w5/d2/p2)

# Week 5, Day 2.2 - Logging in once

Every test in Week 3 signed in first. Six tests, six sign-ins, six times the same three seconds
spent proving something you already proved.

Today: sign in **once**, save the session to a file, hand that file to every test.

> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

## What a browser actually remembers

"Being logged in" is not a state inside Playwright. It is data the site left in your browser:

| Where | Typically holds |
|---|---|
| Cookies | a session id |
| `localStorage` | a token, user preferences |
| `sessionStorage` | shorter-lived tokens |

Playwright can copy all three out to a JSON file and pour them back into a fresh browser later.
That file is called **storage state**.

> **Site note:** today uses `saucedemo.com`, not the banking app. The banking app keeps *no*
> cookies and *nothing* in either storage - so there is nothing to save and the technique cannot
> be shown on it. Finding that out took one probe; it is a reasonable first check before planning
> any auth work.

## Step 2 - the setup file

A normal script: launch a browser by hand, sign in, save, close. Not a test - no `test()` call
anywhere in it.

Read its last two lines again:

```ts
await page.waitForURL(/inventory/);                    // proof the login worked
await page.context().storageState({ path: STATE_FILE });
```

The `waitForURL` is not decoration. Save before the login completes and you write a file full of
nothing - and every test then fails for a reason that looks nothing like *setup was too fast*.

## Step 3 - the config that ties them together

```ts
globalSetup: "./day2-auth.setup.ts",
use: {
  baseURL: "https://www.saucedemo.com",
  storageState: path.join(__dirname, ".auth", "saucedemo.json"),
},
```

One runs first; the other feeds every browser it creates.

> `.auth/` is git-ignored. A storage-state file is a live credential - committing one hands your
> session to everyone with repo access.

**Four tests, no login step in any of them.** Read the spec: not one `fill()` of a password.

## Step 4 - prove the file is doing the work

A passing test is not proof. These would also pass if saucedemo let anyone browse the inventory.
So build a browser **without** the state and check it is refused - that is Step 4 in the spec you
just ran:

```ts
const anon = await browser.newContext({ storageState: undefined });
await anon.newPage().goto("/inventory.html");
await expect(page.locator(".inventory_item")).toHaveCount(0);   // 0, not 6
```

| Context | `.inventory_item` count |
|---|---|
| default (state loaded) | **6** |
| `storageState: undefined` | **0** |

Six versus zero. Now you know.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 5 - why this file is not named `.spec.ts`

It is `day2-storage-state.authdemo.ts`. Deliberately: it needs `globalSetup` to have run, so
under the repo's normal config it fails 3 of 4 tests. Naming it outside the default `testMatch`
keeps a plain `npx playwright test` green while this lesson still runs on demand.

Do the same for any spec that requires a config the default run does not provide.

## When *not* to do this

| Situation | Why storage state hurts |
|---|---|
| Testing the login form itself | you would be skipping the thing under test |
| Tests need different roles | one shared file means one shared user - save one per role |
| Sessions expire in minutes | the file goes stale mid-run; refresh per file instead |
| Tests mutate the user's data | they now interfere with each other through the shared account |

That last row is the one that bites. Isolation you got for free from a fresh browser does **not**
extend to a shared server-side account.

**Next:** [Day 2.3 - How a real repo does it](/learn/w5/d2/p3)

# Week 5, Day 2.3 - How a real repo does it

Same `storageState`, same saved file - arranged so setup failures are visible and each role gets
its own session.

## The problem with `globalSetup`: it is invisible when it breaks

`globalSetup` runs outside the reporter. No trace, no retry, no line in the HTML report. When the
login page changes, your whole suite fails with a message about a missing file.

The fix: make setup **a test**, in its own project.

## Several roles

One file per role, one project per role:

```
.auth/
  admin.json
  customer.json
```

```ts
projects: [
  { name: "setup", testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ },
  { name: "admin",    use: { storageState: ".auth/admin.json" },
    testMatch: /.*\.admin\.spec\.ts/,    dependencies: ["setup"] },
  { name: "customer", use: { storageState: ".auth/customer.json" },
    testMatch: /.*\.customer\.spec\.ts/, dependencies: ["setup"] },
],
```

A test's filename now decides who it runs as. No `beforeEach` login anywhere.

Look at the third line. `login.spec.ts` matches **neither** project, so it silently never runs -
no error, no warning, just missing coverage. That is the cost of letting a filename decide the
role, and the reason to keep one catch-all project or a test that counts your specs.

## Per-test override

Any single test can opt out or swap user without touching the config:

```ts
test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } });   // start signed out
test.use({ storageState: ".auth/admin.json" });             // just this file, as admin
```

`test.use` at the top of a `describe` applies to that block only. This is how you test the login
form itself inside a suite that otherwise skips login.

## Keeping it from rotting

| Risk | What a real repo does |
|---|---|
| File committed by accident | `.auth/` in `.gitignore`; check with `git check-ignore -v <path>` |
| Stale session | regenerate every run; never cache between CI jobs |
| Setup passes but saves nothing | assert *after* login and *before* saving |
| Shared account, mutating tests | one account per worker, or read-only tests only |

**Next:** [Day 2.4 - Practice](/learn/w5/d2/p4)

# Week 5, Day 2.4 - Practice

Work in `week5/generated/`. Copy the three Day 2 files to new names first.

Everything here uses `saucedemo.com`, whose usernames are listed on its own login page.
**Next:** [Day 3.1 - Prerequisites](/learn/w5/d3/p1)

problems.statement:
**Read the file you generated**
Open `week5/generated/.auth/saucedemo.json` and find where the session actually lives - cookie,
`localStorage`, or both.

**Right when:** you can name the one key that makes the difference, and say what would happen if
you deleted it.

**Corrupt it deliberately**
Change one character inside that value, then run the spec.

**Right when:** tests fail, and you can say which of the four failed *first* and why. Restore the
file by re-running the setup.

**A second role**
`saucedemo.com` has a `problem_user`. Write a second setup file that signs in as them and saves
to `.auth/problem.json`, plus a config that uses it.

**Right when:** a test asserting 6 inventory items passes for both users - and you can say which
account you would expect to break a *UI* test first, given its name.

**Delete the save line**
Comment out `storageState({ path: ... })` in your copy of the setup, delete the JSON file, and
run.

**Right when:** the failure points at a missing file, and you can say why that message is *worse*
than a failing setup test would be.

**Remove the wait**
Delete `await page.waitForURL(/inventory/)` from your setup. Run it, then inspect the saved JSON.

**Right when:** you can show - from the file's contents, not from the test output - that it was
written too early.

**Sign out inside a test**
Add a test that signs out, and a second test that expects to still be signed in.

**Right when:** both pass. Explain in one line why signing out in one test cannot affect the
other, but changing the user's *cart on the server* would.

**Convert to a setup project**
Rewrite your Day 2 setup as a `.setup.ts` **test** with a setup project and `dependencies`, per
[day2_3](/learn/w5/d2/p3). Then break the password on purpose.

**Right when:** the HTML report shows a failing test named `authenticate` - not a mystery
missing-file error. This is the payoff of the whole lesson.
